newsitem.title: USA: U.S. warns South Africa on arms sales.
newsitem.headline: U.S. warns South Africa on arms sales.

text.p: The United States on Monday threatened to cut aid to South Africa if Pretoria follows through with reported plans to sell arms to Syria.

"We are deeply concerned about these reports. It would be extremely serious if these sales actually occurred," State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns told reporters. "The United States hopes that the South African government will not consummate arms sales to a country that supports terrorists."

Burns warned that "both the foreign operations and foreign assistance acts -- the law of the United States -- prohibits certain forms of U.S. assistance to governments which supply lethal equipment to Syria or any other countries listed by the United States as state sponsors of terrorism."
"We would certainly analyse any potential sales in the context of our laws. It's a matter of very serious concern," he said, adding: "This is at the top of our agenda with South Africa now."
Officials in Johannesburg said on Sunday that South Africa was considering selling weapons systems, including tank firing systems, worth three billion rand ($641 million) to Syria.

The tough public warning was unusual. Washington has frowned on previous South African deals -- with Iran, for instance -- but mostly muted its criticism out of respect and support for President Nelson Mandela and his country's great strides toward democracy after years of racial segregation known as apartheid.

The White House also expressed its opposition to the reported arms sales to Syria. "We have a strongly worded statement here that amounts to saying we think that's a very bad idea," White House spokesman Mike McCurry told reporters.

McCurry said the administration has "not independently confirmed that they may be trying to transfer tank firing missile systems to Syria but we urge the government of South Africa not to go through with the sale."
"We have confidence that the government of South Africa understands the seriousness of this issue," he said.
South Africa, a major U.S. aid recipient, is due to receive $120 million in 1996-97.

Burns said he did not know how much might be affected by the arms sale. He said that would depend in part on the exact nature of the sale, adding that U.S. officials have many questions about the deal and are seeking answers.
Despite this apparent lack of concrete independent information, Burns said the State Department had known about the deal for a while and had had high-level contacts with South African officials.

Johannesburg's Sunday Times said the South African Cabinet had given conditional approval for the supply of tank firing systems to the Damascus government, which is listed by the United States along with Iran, Iraq, Libya, North Korea and Sudan as a "state sponsor of terrorism."

The Cabinet, fearing the move could anger Washington, "made its support conditional on the approval of Deputy President Thabo Mbeki, who was not at the meeting at which the issue was discussed," the newspaper said.

Mbeki was studying the matter and was expected to decide by the first Cabinet meeting of the new year on Jan. 22, his spokesman told Reuters. "He will have studied the matter by then and will raise it and hopefully a decision would be made at that time," spokesman Ricky Naidoo said.

A source close to the South African state weapons agency said the equipment in question was an electronic system for computerized control of the mechanism that fires the cannon in tanks and howitzers.
